newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM rejects offer to join rival alliance.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM rejects offer to join rival alliance.

text.p: Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen on Friday rejected an offer to join an alliance headed by his main rival in the coalition government.
But the co-premier said his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) wanted to continue working with the royalist FUNCINPEC party of First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh in government and parliament.

"The CPP cannot join with any front because we are the CPP, a big party, and we cannot accept to join with any front, but we can cooperate with any party," he told reporters on the opening day of the annual CPP congress.
"We continue with FUNCINPEC in government, in the national assembly, and we want to cooperate for the future," he said.
Hun Sen said the CPP had no plans to form its own alliance, as some analysts have predicted.
But he confirmed that representatives from former Khmer Rouge military units were attending the four-day congress.
The Khmer Rouge, who ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979 and launched a reign of terror that left more than one million people dead, have been crippled by thousands of defections since last August.

Ranariddh on Thursday confirmed plans to form a new political grouping, including Khmer Rouge defectors and the opposition Khmer Nation Party, and said the CPP could join the alliance, called the Front Uni National (FUN -- United National Front).
The prince denied it was aimed against the CPP, but analysts said the front would exacerbate tension in the uneasy coalition and could paralyse government more than one year before elections are due.
Some believe Ranariddh offered to include the CPP in the new alliance, which is expected to be formally launched next month, knowing that it would not accept.
"There will be tension, more tension. This is not going to solve anything," one diplomat said.

"This is like someone married," said member of parliament Ahmad Yahya. "The husband has an affair with someone and the wife has an affair with someone else and they announce it publicly, so the marriage becomes sour, paralysed."

FUNCINPEC and the formerly communist CPP formed an alliance after U.N.-run elections in 1993, but relations have been strained by the royalists demanding a greater share of power and by the two parties vying for the allegiance of defectors.
Ranariddh said on Thursday the front's charter was "aimed at unifying all of the Cambodians...all the points raised in the charter are really vital issues for Cambodia."
But some analysts believe it is aimed at boosting FUNCINPEC's chances in the polls.
Cambodia is due to be led by one prime minister after the elections next year, and both premiers have predicted victory.
But Hun Sen reiterated that Cambodia, which emerged from years of war on the signing of a U.N.-brokered peace accord in 1991, needed a coalition for at least 10 more years.
